prompt.context: Our client, Bell Computer Inc., is the second largest PC manufacturer, by unit sales, in the United States. Over the past 5 years, Bell has been gaining market share and growing revenue, but at the same time, their net income is eroding. The founder of Bell has returned to the company and taken over as CEO. He has hired us to determine two things.
prompt.question: (1) Why have our profit margins declined? (2) What can we do to improve our profitability and reach our 'Full Potential'?

clarifying_info.a: ASP, or Average Selling Price, is the average price at which the company sells a computer. Multiplying units sold by ASP gives total revenue.
PCs designed for and sold to retail consumers, either direct or through a retailer like Best Buy.
Assume only hardware is sold as shown in Exhibit 1 (Desktop PCs, Laptop PCs, Netbook PCs, Servers, Other). Other products include Pocket PCs and Calculators.
This is a US domestic decision only. Ignore international.

clarifying_info.q: How do Bell's prices compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: All competitors face the same ASPs and sell comparable products.

exhibits.title: Product Mix breakdown by Business Segment for 2005 and 2010
exhibits.shows: Two pie charts showing PC units (thousands) sold by product type (Desktop PCs, Laptop PCs, Netbook PCs, Servers, Other) in 2005 and 2010. Netbook PCs did not exist in 2005. 'Other' products include Pocket PCs and Calculators.
exhibits.data: 2005: Desktop 20K, Laptop 10K, Netbook 0K, Servers 5K, Other 5K, Total 40K. 2010: Desktop 30K, Laptop 30K, Netbook 5K, Servers 10K, Other 5K, Total 80K.

exhibits.title: ASPs by Business Segment 2005 and 2010
exhibits.shows: Bar or table chart showing Average Selling Prices by product segment for 2005 and 2010. Netbook PCs did not exist in 2005.
exhibits.data: 2005 ASPs: Desktop $1,000, Laptop $2,000, Netbook N/A, Servers $3,000, Other $250. 2010 ASPs: Desktop $1,000, Laptop $750, Netbook $500, Servers $3,000, Other $250.

exhibits.title: Avg. Per Unit Cost Breakdown of a Desktop PC for Bell (2005, 2010) and Top 3 Competitors
exhibits.shows: A cost breakdown table comparing per-unit costs (CPU/Cost Per Unit) for Bell in 2005, Bell in 2010, and Bell's top 3 competitors (Haysus, Racer, HC), segmented by cost line items (parts procurement, direct labor, G&A, etc.). Note: Servers, Laptops, and Netbook product types have the same costs per unit as Desktops; 'Other' products have a total CPU of $200.
exhibits.data: Bell 2005 CPU: $800. Bell 2010 CPU: $800 (unchanged). Competitors show lower costs in specific line items: Haysus has lower parts/procurement cost, Racer has lower direct labor, HC has lower G&A. Full Potential CPU (best-of-breed across competitors): $350 for Desktop/Laptop/Netbook/Servers; $200 for Other.

framework: Frame as a Profit Equation: Profit/Unit = Price/Unit (ASP) - Variable Cost/Unit - Fixed Costs/Unit
Compare 2005 vs 2010 financials across all product segments
Analyze Revenue drivers: unit volume changes and ASP changes by product type
Analyze Cost drivers: cost per unit by product type and total costs
Calculate Net Income per unit, total revenue, total cost, and total net income for 2005 and 2010
Identify root causes of margin erosion from the above analysis
Benchmark Bell's costs against top competitors to identify 'Full Potential' improvements
Quantify the net income improvement achievable at Full Potential

questions.prompt: Using Exhibits 1 and 2, explain why Bell's profit margins have declined from 2005 to 2010.
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies three compounding factors: (1) product mix shift toward Laptops and new Netbooks which have lower/negative margins at current costs; (2) Laptop ASP declined sharply from $2,000 to $750; (3) Bell's cost per unit remained flat at $800 despite falling prices, making Laptops and Netbooks loss-making. Revenue grew but net income fell because high-margin Desktops became a smaller share, and new volume came from low/negative-margin products.

math.setup: Calculate NI/Unit = ASP - CPU for each product type and year, then Revenue = Units x ASP, Total Cost = Units x CPU, NI = Revenue - Total Cost.
steps: BELL FY2005: Desktop NI/Unit=$1,000-$800=$200; Laptop NI/Unit=$2,000-$800=$1,200; Servers NI/Unit=$3,000-$800=$2,200; Other NI/Unit=$250-$200=$50
BELL FY2005 Total NI: Desktop $4.0M + Laptop $12.0M + Servers $11.0M + Other $0.3M = $27.3M; Profit Margin 48.4%
BELL FY2010: Desktop NI/Unit=$1,000-$800=$200; Laptop NI/Unit=$750-$800=-$50; Netbook NI/Unit=$500-$800=-$300; Servers NI/Unit=$3,000-$800=$2,200; Other NI/Unit=$250-$200=$50
BELL FY2010 Total NI: Desktop $6.0M + Laptop -$1.5M + Netbook -$1.5M + Servers $22.0M + Other $0.3M = $25.3M; Profit Margin 29.3%
Net Income declined from $27.3M to $25.3M despite Revenue growing from $56.3M to $86.3M
math.answer: Total net income fell from $27.3M (48.4% margin) in 2005 to $25.3M (29.3% margin) in 2010, driven by Laptop ASP collapse and flat cost structure making Laptops and Netbooks loss-generating products.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, identify how Bell can reach its 'Full Potential' and quantify the improvement.
questions.guidance: Strong answer benchmarks Bell's $800 CPU against best-in-class competitors: adopt Haysus's parts procurement strategy, Racer's direct labor approach, and HC's G&A structure. The combined Full Potential CPU is $350 (vs. current $800), a reduction of $450/unit across Desktop, Laptop, Netbook, and Servers. Calculate the net income at Full Potential and the incremental improvement.

math.setup: Apply Full Potential CPU of $350 to 2010 unit volumes (same ASPs). Calculate NI/Unit, Total NI, and incremental improvement vs. 2010 actuals.
steps: Full Potential CPU: $350 for Desktop/Laptop/Netbook/Servers; $200 for Other (unchanged)
Full Potential NI by segment: Desktop=30K x $650=$19.5M; Laptop=30K x $400=$12.0M; Netbook=5K x $150=$0.75M; Servers=10K x $2,650=$26.5M; Other=5K x $50=$0.3M
Full Potential Total NI = $19.5M + $12.0M + $0.75M + $26.5M + $0.3M = $59.0M; Profit Margin 68.4%
Cost per box reduced by $450/unit across main product lines
NI improvement by segment: Desktop +$13.5M, Laptop +$13.5M, Netbook +$2.25M, Servers +$4.5M, Other $0
math.answer: By reducing CPU from $800 to $350 (saving $450/unit), Bell can reach Full Potential NI of ~$59M (68.4% margin), an improvement of ~$34M versus 2010 actual NI of $25.3M.

brainstorming.prompt: What additional ways could Bell Computer improve its net income beyond cost reduction?

categories.name: Cost reduction levers
ideas: SKU rationalization (reduce number of product models to lower complexity and overhead)
Consolidate supplier base for better volume pricing

categories.name: Revenue and pricing strategies
ideas: Bundle high-margin accessories with PC sales
Target higher-margin enterprise/Servers segment for growth
Introduce tiered pricing or premium product lines

categories.name: Channel and go-to-market
ideas: Reduce reliance on low-margin retail channel, grow direct sales
Partner with corporate IT buyers for bulk sales at better economics

recommendation: Bell's margin erosion is driven by a product mix shift toward Laptops and new Netbooks combined with sharp Laptop ASP declines, while costs remained flat at $800/unit — turning these segments loss-making

Bell should immediately benchmark and adopt best-in-class cost structures from competitors: Haysus's parts procurement, Racer's direct labor model, and HC's G&A approach, reducing CPU from $800 to $350 and unlocking ~$34M in additional net income
risks: Competitor cost advantages may reflect scale, proprietary processes, or geographic sourcing that Bell cannot replicate quickly
Continued ASP pressure across all segments could erode margins further even after cost reduction
Netbook segment may have low long-term viability given rapid market evolution
next_steps: Deep-dive on each competitor's cost advantage to assess feasibility and timeline for Bell to replicate
Develop a SKU rationalization plan to reduce complexity costs
Evaluate cross-sell opportunities in software, warranties, and accessories to diversify revenue mix
